newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG extends mercenary inquiry until May 30.
newsitem.headline: PNG extends mercenary inquiry until May 30.

text.p: An official Papua New Guinea inquiry into the US$36 million mercenary deal which sparked an army revolt, forcing the South Pacific nation's prime minister to step aside, has been extended to May 30.
The six-week extension, announced by acting prime minister John Giheno, means the inquiry will end two weeks before polling begins in a scheduled national election.
"The inquiry must unfold the truth, our names must be cleared before we all go to the polls," Giheno said in a statement. The inquiry had been scheduled to end on Friday.
"The importance of this inquiry cannot be questioned. The whole nation is waiting to know its outcome," he said.
The extension will enable former prime minister Sir Julius Chan to give evidence, but more importantly it may avoid a second army revolt.

Chan and two of his senior ministers stood aside last month after sacked defence force commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded Chan resign over the secret decision to hire mercenaries to put down a rebellion on Bougainville island.
By the time the inquiry now ends and Judge Warwick Andrew completes his report, Papua New Guinea will be on the brink of a national election scheduled to start on June 14.
If the inquiry had ended on Friday, as originally scheduled, and Chan was cleared of wrongdoing, he could have resumed power two months ahead of the elections -- a move the army might have resisted.
Police commissioner Bob Nenta has already called for the military to stay in barracks during the June election, although in the past the defence force has helped police monitor voting.
Troops in Port Moresby last week distributed pamphlets calling on Chan to "totally resign" from power.
The pamphlet claimed Chan and deputy prime minister Chris Haiveta and defence minister Mathias Ijape, who all stepped aside on March 26 pending the inquiry, were still in control.
Singirok on Wednesday stormed out of the inquiry after being called a liar by government counsel and returned to his heavily-guarded home inside army headquarters in Port Moresby.

During five days of testimony from Singirok, government counsel Marshall Cooke tried to cast doubt on Singirok's motives and to portray him as an inept commander whose failures on Bougainville forced Chan to arrange the mercenary contract.
